title: The Night Gallery paintings (1969-1973)
creator: Thomas J. Wright; Jaroslav Gebr (pilot)
description: Every segment of Rod Serling's Night Gallery was introduced by Serling standing beside a painting made for that story; about 101 originals were produced. After the pilot, Universal staff artist Thomas J. Wright painted nearly all of them, mostly in acrylic on Masonite, deliberately changing style from piece to piece so the gallery looked like the work of many artists. After cancellation the canvases were stored by Universal's property department, reused as set dressing (including two Columbo episodes), hung in offices, sold off cheaply, auctioned, or stolen; only a handful remain with the studio.
tz_connection: The paintings were the framing device of Night Gallery, Rod Serling's follow-up anthology to The Twilight Zone, and Serling's on-camera introductions were built around them.
recommendation_reason: The paintings are the visual signature of Serling's second anthology and a major collecting subject; a natural hub page for the Night Gallery art section.

title: The Twilight Zone (1959) season 1 opening title sequence

description: The first opening, used for most of season one, is about 40 seconds of slow, stark black-and-white animation produced by the UPA studio. title: The Twilight Zone seasons 4-5 opening (door, window, eye, E=mc2)
description: The final opening is the most often copied. A line in space becomes a spinning door that the viewer passes through ('the key of imagination'), followed by a shattering window for the dimension of sound, a floating eye that opens for sight, Einstein's E=mc2 for mind, a jointed mannequin for 'shadow and substance', and a ticking clock, before particles form the title and rush toward the camera. No designer is credited in the sources consulted.
tz_connection: The definitive opening of the original series' last two seasons; the 2019 Methodmade titles rework the same imagery.
recommendation_reason: The opening imagery that defines the franchise.

title: Original-series sponsor billboards and IDs (1961-1964)
description: Sponsor IDs and 'brought to you by' billboards ran before the first commercial and after the closing credits. Accounts posted on TV Obscurities list Liggett & Myers' Chesterfield as primary sponsor in 1961-62 (Serling plugged the brand after his next-week preview), Colgate-Palmolive as alternate until early 1962, Carter-Wallace's Arrid as a one-week sponsor, and American Tobacco's Pall Mall with Procter & Gamble (Crest, Prell) in 1963-64.
tz_connection: The sponsor art and announcements that framed original broadcasts.
recommendation_reason: Useful context on broadcast-era advertising, but it rests on a reader's account; verify before publishing.

name: Thomas J. Wright
description: Universal Studios artist who painted almost all of the roughly 101 Night Gallery paintings after the pilot, usually several at once, mostly in acrylic on Masonite, using his daughters and then-wife as models. He started as a concept artist on Hitchcock and Coppola films and went on to direct TV including Castle and Supernatural. He still owns his painting for "The Caterpillar".
tz_connection: Painter of the Night Gallery canvases that Rod Serling introduced on camera.

name: Jaroslav Gebr
description: Czech-born scenic artist (1926-2013) who trained at the Prague Academy of Art, fled Czechoslovakia in 1949, and worked in Munich, Florence and Bogotá before Hollywood. He painted murals for Fantastic Voyage and the Sistine Chapel portraits in The Shoes of the Fisherman, then headed Universal's scenic art department for about 30 years. He painted the Night Gallery pilot work, including "The Escape Route" painting now owned by Guillermo del Toro. The ADG's Gallery 800 held a tribute show in 2017.
tz_connection: Painted the pilot canvases for Rod Serling's Night Gallery (1969).
